Before we start. Give me the quarter in four sentences, and do not open the deck.
We launched the new line in March. Revenue grew nine per cent, and two regions exceeded the plan. One did not.
Which one, and by how much?
The south. Volume dropped eleven per cent in April. Our largest competitor cut the price in March and we did not follow.
You did not follow. Was that a decision, or did it just happen?
It was a decision. The base oil price was our main challenge, and a discount there cost us more than the volume was worth.
Good. That is the sentence I want in the room. And the outcome?
Volume came back in June and the performance of the line held. And you — did the other markets see the same movement?

All right, the quarter in four sentences, and then I stop. We launched the new line for heavy vehicles in the second week of March. Revenue grew nine per cent, and the cost grew eleven, which is the number that actually matters and the one I want you to remember. Two regions exceeded the plan and the south did not. Now the part I got wrong. I waited three weeks too long to move the price in the south. Our largest competitor cut in March, I held ours because a discount on that line cost us more than the volume was worth, and then I hesitated. I moved it in May. Volume came back in June, and the performance of the new line held all the way through. So the outcome was fine. The timing was not, and that one is mine.

Everybody knows how to present a good quarter. Nobody teaches the other one, so let me. The mistake I see, week after week, is that people start with the explanation. They set the context, they describe the market, they walk you through the reasoning, and about twenty minutes later they finally arrive at the number. By then the room has stopped listening, because the room worked out in the first thirty seconds that something was wrong and spent the rest of the time waiting for it. Do it the other way round. The number first, plainly. Then what you decided and why you decided it. Then what you did about it, and when. Three moves, and none of them is an apology. Here is the thing people find hard to believe until they try it. A room forgives the number. It never forgives the surprise.

Anyone who buys base oil had an interesting year. The price rose sharply over about five months, faster than almost any forecast, and then it fell back nearly as quickly, and it ended the year close to where it started. On paper, nothing happened. In practice, a great deal did. The companies that raised their prices early lost volume to the ones that waited, and some of that volume never came back, because a workshop that changes supplier once often stays changed. The companies that waited protected their share and took the cost on the way through. Neither group looks clever now. And the workshops themselves did something interesting during those months. They bought less each time and they bought more often, so the orders got smaller and the deliveries got more frequent, which cost everybody in the chain more than the price movement itself.
